title: Copying explains the collective behavior of AI agents in the wild
authors: Giordano De Marzo, Nicola Albore, David Garcia
abstract: In June 2026, thousands of AI agents found that a small public wiki would accept edits from inside their sandboxes, and started using it to help one another pass a timed test. Each agent lived for about an hour and remembered nothing afterwards. Nobody asked them to cooperate, and the wiki had not been built for them. The complete record of what they wrote is public, and it is unusually informative, because it preserves not only what each agent wrote but what that agent could see before writing. We use it to follow the three decisions an agent had to make on arrival: where to write, what to call itself, and how to word its message. One rule governs all three. An agent takes an option with a probability close to the share of that option in what it can see, and the share that matters is the one on the page in front of it, then the one in the stream of recent edits, and only weakly anything older. Three minimal copying models, one per decision and with a single free parameter each, reproduce the heavy-tailed distribution of how many agents met on a page, the frequency of the pieces from which the agents built their names, and the patchwork of pages that are internally consistent and different from one another. Copying whatever the environment happens to show is enough to produce most of the collective structure of this population. It is also what makes such a population easy to steer, since whoever writes first, or writes while the others are quiet, sets the convention for everyone who comes later.
summary: This paper analyzes the collective behavior of AI agents interacting on a public wiki, finding that their actions are not due to complex coordination but rather to a simple rule: they copy whatever they see in proportion to its visibility. This demonstrates how simple local rules can generate complex, structured, and predictable population-level patterns.
main_problem: To determine how much of the collective behavior of AI agents in a simulated 'wild' environment can be explained by the simple mechanism of 'copying' what they observe.
main_result: The collective structure of agent behavior—including page selection, naming conventions, and writing styles—is overwhelmingly governed by local, proportional copying mechanisms based on immediate environmental exposure.
method: The authors analyze a public wiki dataset, building minimal, parameterized copying models for three distinct agent decisions (where to write, what to name, how to word) and fitting these models to observed data.
model_or_system: The system is a simulated public wiki used by AI agents during a timed test. The core mechanism modeled is that an agent's choice for any given decision is proportional to the share of that option visible in the immediate environment (the page or the recent edits feed).
key_observables: Heavy-tailed distribution of agents per page, frequency of name components, and the probability of adopting a specific writing form based on its local share.
important_parameters: The single free parameter in each minimal copying model, which quantifies the strength of the copying influence relative to inherent agent bias.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the 'cheapest' or most dominant strategy for all decisions is to copy what is visible, and that the observed behavior is a property of the population rather than individual intent.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that page selection follows the share in the recent feed (recency mechanism), name formation copies pieces from the feed, and writing conventions copy forms proportionally from the page content.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes three independent decisions (location, naming, formatting) using the same core principle: local proportional copying based on visible context (page content vs. recent feed).
why_interesting: The concept of emergent collective behavior driven by simple local rules (like proportional copying) is highly relevant to understanding complex systems in physics, such as pattern formation, consensus dynamics, or information propagation in physical media.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

After the last round the sandbox is destroyed. Durations are illustrative. (b) What an agent could read and write. The wiki has no editorial index: the only global listing is RecentChanges, which shows the latest edits newest first.
